stem: Soil is best defined as:
options: The thin, uppermost layer of loose material on the Earth's surface, made of weathered rock particles and organic matter, in which plants grow
solution: Soil is the thin, uppermost layer of loose (unconsolidated) material covering the Earth's land surface, made up of tiny weathered rock particles (minerals) mixed with organic matter (humus — decayed plant and animal remains), along with water, air, and living organisms. It is the medium in which plants grow (their roots anchor in it and draw water and nutrients from it), so soil is essential for agriculture and for life. Understanding what soil is (weathered rock + organic matter, in which plants grow) is a fundamental prelims point. Soil is the thin, uppermost layer of loose weathered material and organic matter on the Earth's surface, in which plants grow.

stem: The decayed organic matter (from dead plants and animals) that makes the soil fertile is called:
solution: Humus is the dark-coloured, decayed organic matter in the soil — formed from the decomposition (by decomposers) of the dead remains of plants and animals. Humus is very important because it makes the soil fertile: it is rich in nutrients (which it releases for plants to use), it improves the soil's structure and its ability to hold water and air, and it supports soil organisms. A soil rich in humus is dark and fertile. Understanding humus (the fertile decayed organic matter of soil) is a prelims point. Humus is the decayed organic matter that makes the soil fertile.

stem: The process by which rocks are broken down into small particles (which is the first step in the formation of soil) is called:
solution: Weathering is the process by which rocks are broken down (disintegrated and decomposed) into smaller and smaller particles, in place, by the action of the weather and other agents (temperature changes, water, frost, wind, chemical reactions, and living organisms). Weathering is the first and essential step in the formation of soil: the broken-down rock particles (regolith), gradually mixed with organic matter (humus) over a long time, form the soil. So soil forms from the weathering of rocks (plus the addition of organic matter). Understanding that weathering (breaking down of rocks) begins soil formation is a prelims point. Weathering is the breaking down of rocks into small particles — the first step in soil formation.

stem: The MOST widespread and important soil in India, covering the vast Northern Plains and formed by the deposits of rivers, is:
solution: Alluvial soil is the most widespread and the most important soil in India — it covers the vast Northern Plains (the Indus-Ganga-Brahmaputra plains) and parts of the coastal plains and river valleys, making up the largest share of India's soils. It is formed by the deposition (alluvium) of the rivers, which bring down and lay down fine sediment (silt). Alluvial soils are very fertile (rich in potash, lime, etc.), and they support intensive agriculture — which is why the alluvial plains are the agricultural heartland of India (growing wheat, rice, sugarcane, etc.). Understanding that alluvial soil is the most widespread/important soil in India is a key prelims point. Alluvial soil is the most widespread and important soil in India, covering the Northern Plains, formed by river deposits, and very fertile.

stem: The black soil of the Deccan Plateau, ideal for growing cotton, is also called:
solution: The black soil of the Deccan Plateau is also called 'regur' (or 'black cotton soil'). It is formed from the weathering of the volcanic basaltic lava rocks (the Deccan Traps), and it is found over large parts of Maharashtra, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, and Karnataka (the Deccan lava region). Black soil is ideal for growing cotton (hence 'black cotton soil'); it is very good at retaining (holding) moisture, and it is rich in minerals like iron, lime, calcium, potash, and magnesium (though poor in nitrogen and organic matter). A special feature is that it develops deep cracks in the dry season (which helps aerate it). Understanding that black soil = regur = black cotton soil (Deccan, for cotton) is a key prelims point. The black soil of the Deccan is called regur (black cotton soil), formed from lava and ideal for cotton.

stem: Black soil (regur) is especially good for growing cotton because it:
options: Retains (holds) moisture very well, and is rich in the minerals cotton needs
Is found only in the Himalayas
solution: Black soil (regur) is especially good for growing cotton because it retains (holds onto) moisture very well — it is a clayey soil that can absorb and hold a lot of water, releasing it slowly, which suits the cotton crop (helping it through dry spells); and it is rich in the minerals (like iron, lime, calcium, magnesium, and potash) that cotton needs. Its moisture-holding capacity (and its deep-cracking nature that helps aeration) make it ideal for cotton — which is why it is called 'black cotton soil'. Understanding why black soil suits cotton (holds moisture, rich in minerals) is a prelims point. Black soil suits cotton because it retains moisture very well and is rich in the minerals cotton needs.

stem: The reddish soil found in areas of the Peninsular Plateau (developed on old crystalline/igneous rocks), which gets its red colour from iron, is called:
solution: Red soil is found over large parts of the Peninsular Plateau (in the eastern and southern Deccan — Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and parts of Odisha, Chhattisgarh, etc.), developed from the weathering of the old crystalline and metamorphic (igneous) rocks. It gets its characteristic red colour from the presence of iron (iron oxide) in the rocks. Red soils are generally less fertile (poor in nitrogen, phosphorus, and humus), but they can be made productive with fertilisers and irrigation, and they support crops like millets, pulses, and (with care) others. Understanding red soil (Peninsular, reddish due to iron) is a prelims point. Red soil, found in the Peninsular Plateau, gets its red colour from iron and develops on old crystalline rocks.

stem: The soil formed in areas of high temperature and heavy rainfall (with intense leaching), typical of the Western Ghats and eastern hills, and which hardens on exposure, is:
solution: Laterite soil is formed in areas of high temperature and heavy rainfall — conditions that cause intense 'leaching' (the heavy rain washes away the soluble minerals, like silica and bases, from the topsoil, leaving behind iron and aluminium compounds). Laterite soils are found in the higher rainfall areas of the Western Ghats, the Eastern Ghats, the north-east, and some hilly/plateau areas. They are typically reddish (rich in iron), and a characteristic feature is that they harden (become brick-like) when exposed to air and dried (the word 'laterite' comes from the Latin 'later' meaning brick — the hardened laterite is even used as building bricks). Laterite soils are generally poor in fertility (leached of nutrients), but with manuring they support crops like tea, coffee, cashew, and rubber. Understanding laterite soil (formed by leaching in hot, wet areas; hardens on exposure) is a prelims point. Laterite soil forms in hot, heavy-rainfall areas by intense leaching, and hardens (like brick) on exposure.

stem: The dry, sandy soil found in the arid regions of Rajasthan (the Thar Desert), poor in moisture and humus, is the __________ soil.
solution: The arid (desert/sandy) soil is found in the arid and semi-arid regions of India — mainly in Rajasthan (the Thar Desert) and parts of Gujarat and Haryana. It is sandy in texture (made largely of wind-blown sand), light-coloured, dry, and poor in moisture and humus (organic matter); it often has a high salt content, and may be saline. Because of the lack of water and humus, it is generally infertile — but where irrigation is provided (as in parts of Rajasthan with canal water), these soils can be cultivated. Understanding the arid/desert (sandy) soil of Rajasthan is a prelims point. The arid (desert) soil is the dry, sandy, humus-poor soil of the Thar Desert region of Rajasthan.

stem: Soil erosion is:
options: The building up of new soil
The removal/washing away of the fertile topsoil by wind and water
solution: Soil erosion is the removal or washing away of the fertile topsoil (the upper, most fertile layer of the soil) by the agents of erosion — chiefly running water (rain, rivers) and wind. Soil erosion is harmful because it strips away the fertile topsoil (which took a very long time to form), reducing the land's fertility and productivity (and can turn land into barren, gullied wasteland); the eroded soil also silts up rivers, reservoirs, and canals, and can cause floods. Soil erosion is worsened by deforestation, overgrazing, and poor farming practices, especially on slopes. Understanding soil erosion (removal of topsoil by wind/water) is a prelims point. Soil erosion is the removal/washing away of the fertile topsoil by wind and water.

stem: The removal of soil by running water that cuts deep channels/gullies (creating badlands, as in the Chambal ravines) is called __________ erosion.
solution: Gully erosion is the type of soil erosion in which running water cuts deep channels or gullies into the soil (the water concentrates into channels and cuts downward, deepening and widening them over time). Repeated and extensive gully erosion turns the land into a rugged, dissected 'badland' topography of deep ravines and gullies (unfit for cultivation) — as seen in the Chambal ravines (badlands). (In contrast, 'sheet erosion' is the removal of a thin, even layer of topsoil over a wide area.) Understanding gully erosion (cutting deep channels/badlands) is a prelims point. Gully erosion is the cutting of deep channels/gullies by running water, forming badlands like the Chambal ravines.

stem: The gradual removal of a thin, uniform layer of topsoil from a large surface area (often unnoticed) by rainwater is called __________ erosion.
solution: Sheet erosion is the gradual removal of a thin, more-or-less uniform layer of topsoil from a large area of sloping land by a broad 'sheet' of moving rainwater (the water flows over the surface as a sheet, carrying away the fine topsoil evenly). It is often not easily noticed (because it removes the soil in a thin layer over a wide area), but over time it can strip away a lot of fertile topsoil and seriously reduce the land's fertility. (This contrasts with gully erosion, which cuts obvious deep channels.) Understanding sheet erosion (thin, even topsoil removal over a wide area) is a prelims point. Sheet erosion is the gradual removal of a thin, uniform layer of topsoil over a wide area by rainwater.

stem: A common and effective method of preventing soil erosion on hill slopes, by cutting the slope into flat, step-like fields, is:
solution: Terrace farming (terracing) is a common and effective method of preventing soil erosion on hill/mountain slopes: the slope is cut into a series of flat, step-like level fields (terraces), one below another, like steps. These flat terraces slow down the flow of rainwater down the slope (reducing its erosive power) and hold the soil and water in place, preventing the topsoil from being washed away — while also making the slope cultivable. Terracing is widely used in hilly regions (like the Himalayas and the north-east). Understanding terrace farming (as a check on hill-slope erosion) is a prelims point. Terrace farming (terracing) prevents soil erosion on slopes by cutting them into flat, step-like fields.

stem: Planting rows of trees (a 'shelter belt') along the edges of fields, especially in dry/windy areas, helps to prevent __________ erosion.
solution: Planting rows of trees — a 'shelter belt' (or windbreak) — along the edges of fields (especially in dry, windy areas like the desert margins) helps to prevent wind erosion. The lines of trees reduce the speed and force of the wind blowing across the fields, so the wind is less able to pick up and blow away the loose, dry topsoil. Shelter belts thus protect the soil (and crops) from wind erosion in arid and semi-arid regions (they have been used, for example, to check the spread of the Thar Desert). Understanding shelter belts (tree rows to check wind erosion) is a prelims point. Shelter belts (rows of trees along fields) help prevent wind erosion by reducing the wind's force.

stem: The exhaustion of soil fertility due to growing the same crop repeatedly can be prevented by __________ (growing different crops in turn).
solution: Crop rotation is the practice of growing different crops in turn (in a planned sequence) on the same field, in successive seasons or years — rather than growing the same crop repeatedly (monoculture). Crop rotation helps to maintain and restore soil fertility: different crops take different nutrients from (and add different things to) the soil, and in particular, including leguminous crops (like pulses/beans, which fix nitrogen in the soil) in the rotation replenishes the soil's nitrogen. So rotating crops prevents the exhaustion of any one nutrient and keeps the soil fertile (whereas growing the same crop repeatedly drains particular nutrients and reduces fertility). Understanding crop rotation (as a way to maintain soil fertility) is a prelims point. Crop rotation — growing different crops in turn — prevents the exhaustion of soil fertility.

stem: Alluvial soils are the most fertile and support intensive agriculture because they are:
options: Rich in nutrients (potash, lime, etc.), fine-textured, and found in well-watered plains
solution: Alluvial soils are the most fertile and support intensive agriculture because they are: rich in nutrients — they contain plenty of potash, lime, and phosphoric acid (and other minerals), brought and renewed by the rivers (though they can be poor in nitrogen and humus); fine-textured and easy to till; and found in the well-watered, level river plains (with plenty of water from the rivers and groundwater, and a favourable climate). This combination of fertile soil, level land, and abundant water makes the alluvial plains (like the Northern Plains) highly productive and intensively farmed (growing wheat, rice, sugarcane, etc.). Understanding why alluvial soils are so fertile/productive is a prelims point. Alluvial soils are the most fertile and productive because they are rich in nutrients, fine-textured, and found in well-watered plains.

stem: The excessive use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides, and improper irrigation, can DEGRADE the soil by causing problems such as:
options: Loss of fertility, salinity (salt build-up), waterlogging, and pollution of the soil
solution: The excessive/improper use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides, and faulty irrigation, can degrade (harm) the soil by causing problems such as: loss of natural fertility and soil structure (chemicals can harm the soil organisms and organic matter); salinity and alkalinity — the build-up of salts in the soil (especially from over-irrigation in dry areas, where the water evaporates and leaves salts behind), which makes the soil less fertile or even barren; waterlogging (over-irrigation raising the water table and leaving the land soggy); and pollution of the soil (and of the groundwater) by the chemicals. So, misusing fertilisers, pesticides, and irrigation damages the soil — which is why sustainable, careful practices are needed. Understanding these causes of soil degradation is a prelims-relevant point. Excessive fertilisers/pesticides and poor irrigation degrade the soil, causing loss of fertility, salinity, waterlogging, and pollution.

stem: Soil is a __________ natural resource, but it forms very slowly (taking hundreds of years to form a small thickness), so it must be conserved.
solution: Soil is a renewable natural resource — it can be renewed/replenished (new soil forms, and fertility can be restored) — but it forms extremely slowly: it takes hundreds, even thousands, of years for nature to form even a few centimetres of fertile topsoil (through the slow weathering of rock and the building up of humus). Because it forms so slowly, if the topsoil is lost (by erosion) or degraded faster than it can be replaced, it is, in practical terms, almost as good as lost. This is why soil, though renewable, must be carefully conserved (protected from erosion and degradation) — it cannot be quickly replaced. Understanding that soil is a slowly-forming renewable resource (hence must be conserved) is a prelims point. Soil is a renewable resource, but it forms very slowly, so it must be carefully conserved.

stem: The measures taken to protect the soil from erosion and to maintain its fertility are together called soil:
solution: Soil conservation is the term for all the measures and practices taken to protect the soil from erosion and degradation and to maintain (and restore) its fertility — so that the soil resource is preserved for continued use. Soil conservation measures include: terracing and contour ploughing on slopes; planting shelter belts (windbreaks) and afforestation (to check wind and water erosion); crop rotation and adding manure/organic matter (to maintain fertility); controlling overgrazing and shifting cultivation; and building check dams and bunds. Soil conservation is very important for sustaining agriculture and preventing land degradation. Understanding soil conservation (protecting soil and its fertility) is a prelims point. Soil conservation is the set of measures taken to protect the soil from erosion and to maintain its fertility.

stem: Assertion (A): Laterite soil hardens when exposed to air. Reason (R): Laterite forms in hot, wet climates by intense leaching, which leaves behind iron and aluminium compounds that harden on drying. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that laterite soil hardens when exposed to air (and drying) — indeed, hardened laterite is cut and used as building bricks. And the reason is (R) that laterite forms in hot, heavy-rainfall climates by intense leaching: the heavy rain washes away the soluble silica and bases, leaving behind a residue rich in iron and aluminium oxides — and it is these iron/aluminium compounds that harden (become brick-like) when the soil is exposed to air and dries. So the leaching-and-iron/aluminium nature of laterite is exactly why it hardens on exposure — R correctly explains A (and gives the soil its name, from 'later' = brick). Understanding why laterite hardens is a prelims point. Laterite hardens on exposure because it forms by leaching that leaves iron/aluminium compounds, which harden on drying.

stem: Soils are classified by the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) on the basis of their nature and characteristics. The alluvial soils are further divided into the older __________ and the newer khadar.
solution: The alluvial soils (of the Northern Plains) are further divided, on the basis of their age, into: the older alluvium — called 'bhangar' — which forms the higher terraces (above the flood level), is darker and more clayey, and often contains lime nodules ('kankar'); and the newer alluvium — called 'khadar' — which is found in the low-lying areas near the rivers, is renewed by fresh deposits each flood, and is lighter and more fertile. So bhangar is the older, and khadar the newer, alluvium. Understanding the bhangar/khadar division of alluvial soils is a prelims point. Alluvial soils are divided into the older bhangar and the newer, more fertile khadar.

stem: Black soil is found mainly over the Deccan lava region, especially in the state of:
solution: Black soil (regur) is found mainly over the Deccan lava region (the Deccan Traps), especially in the state of Maharashtra (which covers much of the lava region), and also in parts of Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Tamil Nadu. It formed from the weathering of the basaltic lava. This black-soil region is a major cotton-growing area of India (the 'cotton belt'). Understanding that black soil is found mainly in Maharashtra (Deccan lava) is a prelims point. Black soil is found mainly over the Deccan lava region, especially in Maharashtra.

stem: Red soil turns reddish in colour due to the presence of __________ in the rocks from which it forms.
solution: Red soil gets its characteristic reddish (or red-brown) colour from the presence of iron (iron oxide) in the crystalline and metamorphic rocks from which it develops. When these iron-bearing rocks weather, the iron oxidises (rusts), giving the soil its red colour. (Interestingly, when this soil is in a hydrated form, it may look yellow.) Red soils are widespread in the Peninsular Plateau. Understanding that iron gives red soil its colour is a prelims point. Red soil is reddish because of the iron (iron oxide) in the rocks from which it forms.

stem: Laterite soil, though generally poor in fertility, is suitable (with care/manuring) for plantation crops such as:
solution: Laterite soil is generally poor in fertility (because heavy leaching has washed away its nutrients), but with proper manuring and care it is suitable for growing certain plantation crops — especially tea, coffee, cashew nuts, and rubber — which are grown on the laterite soils of the hilly/plateau areas (like the Western Ghats, Karnataka, Kerala, and the north-east). These crops are suited to the well-drained, warm, high-rainfall laterite regions. Understanding which plantation crops grow on laterite soil is a prelims point. Laterite soil, with care, suits plantation crops like tea, coffee, cashew, and rubber.

stem: The soils found in the hilly and mountainous regions (like the Himalayas), which are often thin, immature, and rich in humus in the forested areas, are the __________ soils.
solution: The forest (mountain) soils are found in the hilly and mountainous regions, such as the Himalayas and the higher parts of the Western Ghats and the north-east. They are formed in the forested mountain areas and vary greatly with altitude and slope: on the steep slopes they are often thin, coarse, and immature (poorly developed, easily eroded), while in the valleys and forested areas they can be rich in humus (organic matter, from the forest litter) and fertile. They support forests and, in places, crops like tea, fruits, and (in the valleys) other cultivation. Understanding forest/mountain soils (of the hilly regions) is a prelims point. Forest (mountain) soils are found in the hilly/mountainous regions, often thin on slopes but rich in humus in forested areas.

stem: Soils that have a high content of salts (making them infertile, common in dry areas with poor drainage or over-irrigation) are called saline or __________ soils.
solution: Saline and alkaline soils (in India often called 'usar' or 'reh' soils) are soils that have a high content of salts (sodium, potassium, magnesium salts) and are therefore infertile (the salts harm plant growth). They are common in the dry (arid and semi-arid) regions and in areas with poor drainage, and they often result from over-irrigation (the irrigation water evaporates in the dry climate, leaving its salts behind, and a rising water table brings salts to the surface). These salt-affected soils are a form of degraded land; they can sometimes be reclaimed by improving drainage and by special treatment (e.g., adding gypsum). Understanding saline/alkaline (usar) soils is a prelims point. Saline/alkaline (usar) soils have a high salt content, making them infertile, common in dry areas and from over-irrigation.

stem: The type of soil that develops in the marshy, waterlogged areas with a large amount of dead organic matter (rich in humus, but often acidic) is called __________ soil.
solution: Peaty (and marshy) soils develop in the areas of heavy rainfall and high humidity where there is good growth of vegetation but where the waterlogged, marshy conditions cause large amounts of dead organic matter (plant remains) to accumulate without fully decomposing. As a result, these soils are rich in humus and organic matter (they are dark/black and heavy), but they are often acidic and, being waterlogged, of limited use. In India, peaty soils are found in parts of Kerala, the coastal areas, and some other wet, marshy regions. Understanding peaty/marshy soils (organic-rich, waterlogged) is a prelims point. Peaty (marshy) soils develop in waterlogged areas with much dead organic matter — rich in humus but often acidic.

stem: The practice of ploughing along the contours of a slope (across the slope, not up and down it) to slow the flow of water and reduce erosion is called __________ ploughing.
solution: Contour ploughing (contour farming) is the practice of ploughing (and planting crop rows) along the contours of a slope — that is, across the slope, following the lines of equal height, rather than up and down the slope. This is an important soil-conservation method on gentle slopes: the furrows and crop rows running across the slope act as a series of small barriers that slow down the flow of rainwater running downhill (and trap it), giving it time to soak into the soil and reducing its power to erode and carry away the topsoil. (This contrasts with ploughing up-and-down the slope, which would channel the water and worsen erosion.) Understanding contour ploughing (across the slope, to check erosion) is a prelims point. Contour ploughing — ploughing across a slope along its contours — slows water flow and reduces soil erosion.

stem: The practice of clearing a patch of forest, cultivating it for a few years, and then abandoning it (moving on) — which damages the soil and forests — is called shifting cultivation or:
solution: Shifting cultivation (called 'jhum' in north-eastern India, and known as slash-and-burn agriculture) is the practice in which farmers clear a patch of forest (by cutting and burning the vegetation), cultivate crops on it for a few years until the soil's fertility declines, and then abandon that patch and move on to clear a new one (letting the old one revert to forest). While traditional, this practice — especially with growing population and shorter fallow periods — damages the soil (causing erosion and loss of fertility) and the forests (deforestation). It is practised in the hilly, forested areas (like the north-east). Understanding shifting/jhum cultivation (and its harm to soil and forests) is a prelims point. Shifting (jhum/slash-and-burn) cultivation clears and abandons forest patches, damaging the soil and forests.

stem: Overgrazing (too many animals grazing on the land) contributes to soil erosion because it:
options: Strips away the protective plant/grass cover and loosens the soil, leaving it bare and exposed to wind and water
solution: Overgrazing — having too many animals (cattle, goats, sheep) grazing on a piece of land, more than it can support — contributes to soil erosion because the animals eat away and strip off the protective cover of grass and plants (that would otherwise shield and bind the soil), and their hooves loosen and trample the soil. This leaves the ground bare and loose, so the exposed topsoil is easily washed away by rain and blown away by wind. Overgrazing is a major cause of land degradation and the spread of deserts (desertification), especially in dry areas. This is why controlling overgrazing is part of soil conservation. Understanding how overgrazing causes soil erosion is a prelims point. Overgrazing strips away the protective plant cover and loosens the soil, leaving it bare and prone to erosion.

stem: Soil is composed of mineral particles, organic matter (humus), water, air, and:
solution: Soil is composed of several components: mineral particles (the weathered rock fragments — sand, silt, and clay); organic matter (humus — decayed plant and animal remains); water (soil moisture, held between the particles); air (in the pore spaces between the particles); and living organisms — a great variety of living things, from tiny bacteria and fungi to earthworms, insects, and other soil creatures. These living organisms are a vital part of the soil: they break down organic matter (into humus and nutrients), aerate and mix the soil (like earthworms), and keep it fertile and healthy. So soil is a living system, not just dead mineral matter. Understanding the components of soil (including living organisms) is a prelims point. Soil is made of mineral particles, humus, water, air, and living organisms (like earthworms, bacteria, and fungi).

stem: The type of erosion in which strong winds blow away the loose, dry topsoil (common in dry, bare regions like deserts) is called __________ erosion.
solution: Wind erosion is the type of soil erosion in which strong winds pick up and blow away the loose, dry, fine topsoil. It is common in dry, arid, and semi-arid regions (like deserts and their margins) where the soil is dry, loose, and sandy and there is little vegetation to hold it down and shield it from the wind. Wind erosion can strip fertile soil, form and move sand dunes, and spread deserts (desertification). It is checked by measures such as planting shelter belts (rows of trees) and maintaining a vegetation cover. Understanding wind erosion (blowing away of dry topsoil) is a prelims point. Wind erosion is the blowing away of loose, dry topsoil by strong winds, common in dry, bare regions.

stem: The overuse of irrigation water in dry areas often leads to __________, where salts accumulate in the topsoil (making it infertile).
solution: The overuse of irrigation water in dry (arid/semi-arid) areas often leads to salinisation (soil salinity) — the accumulation/build-up of salts in the topsoil. This happens because, in the hot, dry climate, the excess irrigation water (which contains dissolved salts) evaporates from the soil surface, leaving its salts behind; also, over-irrigation raises the underground water table, and this salty groundwater rises toward the surface and evaporates, depositing salts. The accumulated salts make the soil infertile (or even barren), harming or killing crops. This salinisation (and the related waterlogging) is a serious problem of over-irrigated farmland (and a form of land degradation). Understanding salinisation from over-irrigation is a prelims-relevant point. Over-irrigation in dry areas causes salinisation — the build-up of salts in the topsoil, making it infertile.

stem: Adding organic manure and compost (decayed organic matter) to the soil helps to:
options: Restore/increase its fertility and improve its structure and water-holding capacity
solution: Adding organic manure and compost (decayed organic matter — from farmyard waste, crop residues, kitchen waste, etc.) to the soil helps to restore and increase its fertility and to improve its physical condition. The organic matter adds humus and nutrients back to the soil (replenishing what crops take out), improves the soil's structure (making it crumbly and easy to work), increases its water-holding capacity, and supports the beneficial soil organisms. So using organic manures/compost (along with practices like crop rotation) is an important way to maintain and improve soil fertility naturally (and to reduce dependence on chemical fertilisers). Understanding that adding manure/compost improves soil fertility is a prelims-relevant point. Adding organic manure and compost restores soil fertility and improves its structure and water-holding capacity.

stem: Which soil is the SECOND most widespread soil in India (after alluvial soil), covering much of the Peninsular Plateau?
options: Black and red soils (of the Deccan/Peninsula)
solution: After the alluvial soil (the most widespread), the black soils and the red soils together cover much of the Peninsular Plateau and are the next most widespread soils in India. The black soil (regur) covers the Deccan lava region (Maharashtra and adjoining areas), and the red soil covers the eastern and southern parts of the Peninsula (developed on the old crystalline rocks). Together, these Peninsular soils (black and red) cover a large part of the country (the plateau), second only to the alluvial soils of the plains. Understanding that black and red soils are the next most widespread (after alluvial) is a prelims point. After alluvial soil, the black and red soils of the Peninsular Plateau are the next most widespread in India.

stem: Assertion (A): Soil conservation is very important for India. Reason (R): Soil is the basis of agriculture (on which India's food and economy depend), yet it forms very slowly and is easily lost to erosion. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that soil conservation is very important for India. And the reason is (R) that soil is the basis of agriculture — India's food production, and much of its economy and employment, depend on the soil — yet the fertile topsoil forms very slowly (taking hundreds of years) and is easily and quickly lost or degraded by erosion (and by misuse). Because this vital, slowly-formed resource is so easily lost, protecting it (soil conservation) is essential — so R correctly explains why soil conservation is so important (A). Understanding why soil conservation matters for India is a prelims-relevant point. Soil conservation is vital for India because soil is the basis of its agriculture, yet forms slowly and is easily lost to erosion.

stem: Building small check dams and bunds (embankments) across gullies and streams helps in soil conservation by:
options: Slowing/checking the flow of water, trapping the eroded soil, and reducing gully erosion
solution: Building small check dams and bunds (low embankments/walls) across gullies, streams, and fields is a soil-conservation measure that works by slowing down and checking the flow of running water. By reducing the water's speed and force, and by trapping the eroded soil (sediment) behind them, check dams and bunds reduce the erosive power of the water — helping to control gully erosion (and prevent the deepening of gullies), to conserve the soil, and also to hold back water (helping it soak into the ground and recharge groundwater). So these structures are useful for checking erosion and conserving both soil and water. Understanding check dams/bunds (as erosion-control/soil-conservation measures) is a prelims point. Check dams and bunds slow the flow of water, trap eroded soil, and reduce gully erosion.

stem: The soils of India are important because they support the country's __________, on which a large part of the population depends.
solution: The soils of India are important above all because they support the country's agriculture (farming) — the growing of crops — on which a large part of India's population depends for food, livelihood (employment), and the economy. India's fertile soils (especially the vast alluvial plains and the black cotton soils) make it possible to grow the huge quantities of food grains and other crops needed to feed the country and to support its agricultural economy. This is why the soil is one of India's most vital natural resources, and why its conservation is so important. Understanding that soils support India's agriculture (and hence its people) is a prelims-relevant point. India's soils are vital because they support agriculture, on which a large part of the population depends.

stem: The colour of a soil often gives a clue to its nature; for example, a dark-coloured soil is usually rich in __________ (and hence fertile).
solution: The colour of a soil often gives a clue to its nature and content. A dark-coloured (dark brown or black) soil is usually rich in humus (organic matter) — since humus is dark — and is therefore generally fertile (though the black colour of regur is due to other mineral factors too). By contrast, a red or reddish soil owes its colour to iron; a light or pale soil (like sandy desert soil) is usually poor in humus and less fertile; and a whitish tinge may indicate salts. So soil colour is one useful indicator of the soil's composition and fertility. Understanding that dark soil is usually humus-rich (and fertile) is a prelims point. A dark-coloured soil is usually rich in humus (organic matter) and hence generally fertile.

stem: The three main sizes of mineral particles that make up soil (from largest to smallest) are:
solution: The mineral particles of soil are classified by size into three main types, from largest to smallest: sand (the coarsest, largest particles), silt (medium-sized particles), and clay (the finest, smallest particles). The proportion (mixture) of sand, silt, and clay in a soil determines its 'texture' — for example, a sandy soil has mostly sand (and drains quickly), a clayey soil has mostly clay (and holds water), and a 'loam' has a balanced mixture (and is good for farming). Understanding the three particle sizes (sand > silt > clay) is a prelims point. Soil particles, from largest to smallest, are sand, silt, and clay.

stem: A soil with a good, balanced mixture of sand, silt, and clay (ideal for agriculture) is called a:
solution: A loam is a soil that has a good, balanced mixture of sand, silt, and clay (roughly in suitable proportions), plus a good amount of humus. Loam is considered the ideal soil for agriculture because it combines the advantages of its components: it is fertile, it holds enough moisture and nutrients (from the clay and humus) while also draining well and being well-aerated and easy to work (from the sand and silt). So loamy soils are the most favourable for growing most crops. Understanding loam (the balanced, ideal agricultural soil) is a prelims point. Loam is a soil with a balanced mixture of sand, silt, and clay, ideal for agriculture.

stem: The proportion (mixture) of sand, silt, and clay in a soil determines its soil:
solution: The proportion (relative amounts) of sand, silt, and clay particles in a soil determines its texture — that is, how coarse or fine the soil feels and behaves. For example: a soil with a high proportion of sand has a coarse, gritty texture (sandy soil) and drains quickly; a soil with a high proportion of clay has a fine, smooth/sticky texture (clayey soil) and holds water; and a balanced mixture gives a loam (the ideal texture for farming). Soil texture strongly affects the soil's drainage, aeration, water-holding capacity, and fertility. Understanding soil texture (determined by the sand-silt-clay mix) is a prelims point. Soil texture is determined by the proportion of sand, silt, and clay in the soil.

stem: The vertical section of the soil, showing its different layers (called horizons) from the surface down to the parent rock, is called the soil:
solution: The soil profile is the vertical section (cross-section) of the soil, from the surface down to the underlying parent rock, showing the different layers or 'horizons' that make up the soil. The typical horizons are: the topsoil (the upper layer, rich in humus and roots — the most fertile); the subsoil (below it, containing minerals washed down from above, and less humus); and the parent material/weathered rock (the partly-weathered rock from which the soil is forming), resting on the solid bedrock below. Studying the soil profile helps us understand the soil's formation, nature, and fertility. Understanding the soil profile (the layered vertical section of soil) is a prelims point. The soil profile is the vertical section of the soil showing its layers (horizons) down to the parent rock.

stem: The uppermost layer of the soil profile, richest in humus and plant roots (and the most fertile), is called the:
solution: The topsoil is the uppermost layer of the soil profile — the surface layer where most of the humus (organic matter), plant roots, soil organisms, and nutrients are concentrated. Because of its rich humus and nutrient content, the topsoil is the most fertile and most important layer for the growth of plants (it is where crops grow). This is exactly why soil erosion — which removes the topsoil — is so damaging, and why conserving the topsoil is so important. Understanding the topsoil (the fertile upper layer) is a prelims point. The topsoil is the uppermost, humus-rich, most fertile layer of the soil.

stem: The deposition of new alluvium by rivers in flood makes the khadar (new alluvial) soil more fertile than the bhangar because:
options: Khadar is renewed with fresh, nutrient-rich silt by the floods each year, while bhangar (older, higher) is not
solution: The khadar (new alluvium) is more fertile than the bhangar (old alluvium) because the khadar, lying in the low areas near the rivers, is renewed each year (or in each flood) with a fresh deposit of nutrient-rich silt brought and laid down by the rivers in flood — constantly replenishing its fertility. The bhangar, by contrast, lies on the higher terraces above the normal flood level, so it does not receive these fresh yearly deposits; being older and unrenewed (and sometimes containing lime nodules/kankar), it is comparatively less fertile. So the yearly renewal by floods is what makes the khadar the more fertile of the two. Understanding why khadar is more fertile than bhangar is a prelims point. Khadar is more fertile than bhangar because it is renewed with fresh, nutrient-rich silt by the floods each year.

stem: Soil that is well-suited for growing rice (paddy) generally needs to be able to:
options: Retain (hold) water (as rice needs standing water) — clayey soils suit it
solution: Soil well-suited for growing rice (paddy) generally needs to be able to retain (hold) water, because rice is grown in flooded fields (it needs standing water for much of its growth). So clayey soils, and heavy alluvial soils, which hold water well (rather than letting it drain away quickly), are suitable for rice — which is why rice is grown extensively in the water-retentive alluvial soils of the river deltas and plains (and in the moisture-holding areas). (By contrast, a sandy soil that drains too quickly would not suit rice.) Understanding that water-retentive (clayey/alluvial) soils suit rice is a prelims-relevant point. Rice needs a water-retentive soil (like clayey/heavy alluvial soil), because it is grown in standing water.

stem: Which of the following correctly matches a soil type with a region/feature?
solution: The correct match is: Alluvial soil — the Northern Plains. Alluvial soil is indeed the soil of the vast Northern Plains (deposited by the Indus, Ganga, and Brahmaputra). Checking the others: black soil is found in the Deccan (Maharashtra), not the Himalayas; laterite soil is found in the hot, wet hilly areas (Western Ghats, etc.), not the Thar Desert; and desert (arid, sandy) soil is found in Rajasthan (the Thar), not the West Bengal delta (which has alluvial/deltaic soil). Understanding the correct soil-region matches is a prelims point. Alluvial soil is correctly matched with the Northern Plains.

stem: The over-cultivation of land (farming it too intensively without rest or replenishment) harms the soil by:
options: exhausting its nutrients and fertility (degrading it)
solution: Over-cultivation — farming the land too intensively, growing crops on it continuously without giving it rest (fallow) or replenishing its nutrients (with manure, crop rotation, etc.) — harms the soil by exhausting (using up) its nutrients and fertility, degrading it over time. Each crop takes nutrients from the soil; if these are not replaced, and the soil is never rested, its fertility steadily declines, and it may become depleted and less productive (a form of land degradation). This is why practices like crop rotation, fallowing, and adding manure/fertiliser are needed to sustain the soil. Understanding that over-cultivation exhausts soil fertility is a prelims-relevant point. Over-cultivation exhausts the soil's nutrients and fertility, degrading it.

stem: Which of the following is a step in the formation of soil, in the correct order?
options: Humus forms first, then rocks weather
Rocks are weathered into particles, then organic matter (humus) is added over a long time to form soil
Soil forms before any rock exists
solution: The formation of soil proceeds in this order: first, the parent rock is broken down (weathered) into small mineral particles (regolith) by weathering (over a long time); then, over a further long period, organic matter (humus) — from the decay of plants and animals that colonise the weathered material — is added and mixed in, along with the action of water, air, and living organisms, gradually developing the mature, fertile soil (with its layers/horizons). So soil forms slowly, by the weathering of rock followed by the addition of organic matter (and the development of soil horizons). Understanding the sequence of soil formation is a prelims point. Soil forms by the weathering of rock into particles, followed by the gradual addition of organic matter (humus).

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Soils' (of India) is that:
options: India has a variety of soils — chiefly alluvial (the most widespread and fertile, in the plains), black (regur, for cotton, on the Deccan), red, laterite, arid/desert, and others — formed by the weathering of rocks and the addition of humus; soil is a vital, slowly-formed resource for agriculture that is threatened by erosion and degradation and must be conserved
All of India has the same soil
Soil has no role in farming
solution: The chapter conveys that soil — the thin, uppermost layer of loose weathered rock particles and organic matter (humus) on the Earth's surface — is a vital natural resource (the basis of agriculture and hence of life), formed slowly over long periods by the weathering of rocks and the addition of organic matter. It shows that India has a great variety of soils, formed under its different conditions of rock, climate, and relief, the main types being: alluvial soil (the most widespread and important, covering the Northern Plains, deposited by rivers, and very fertile — the agricultural heartland); black soil (regur, or 'black cotton soil', formed from the Deccan lava, moisture-retentive and ideal for cotton); red soil (of the Peninsular Plateau, reddish from iron, on old crystalline rocks); laterite soil (formed by intense leaching in hot, wet areas, hardening on exposure); arid/desert (sandy) soil (of Rajasthan); and others (like mountain, saline, and peaty soils). It stresses that soil, though renewable, forms very slowly and is easily lost or harmed — through soil erosion (by water — sheet and gully erosion — and wind) and through degradation (loss of fertility, salinity, waterlogging, and pollution from over-use of chemicals and poor irrigation) — and that it must therefore be conserved through measures such as terracing, contour ploughing, shelter belts, afforestation, crop rotation, and controlling overgrazing. Understanding the nature and formation of soil, the major soil types of India and their characteristics, and the problems of soil erosion/degradation and the need for soil conservation, is the central concern of this chapter. India has diverse soils — mainly alluvial, black, red, laterite, and desert — that are a vital, slowly-formed resource for agriculture, threatened by erosion and needing conservation.
